extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, legal theorists, law students, and policymakers interested in democratic legitimacy of administrative institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and design criteria for grounding administrative-state decisionmaking in democratic theory, with a focus on an 'agonistic' model that centers contestation rather than consensus. Targets institutional design features (rulemaking, review, participation, hierarchical structure, inclusion) that affect democratic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy through agonistic unsettlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agonism finds legitimacy in “unsettlement” of the law rather than in achieving societal consensus; legitimacy arises from fostering ongoing contestation where winners and losers alike can practice democracy by defending and critiquing the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage institutional features that sustain contestation and enable continual challenge to 'settled' decisions; value mechanisms that permit political struggle as a source of democratic legitimacy rather than measures that aim to eliminate conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continual justification of settled decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative agon would focus much more than existing administrative processes on forcing agencies to continually justify 'settled' decisions and promote robust adversarial contestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedures and review practices that require agencies to rearticulate and defend past decisions on an ongoing basis (not merely once), thereby preventing ossification and enabling renewed public challenge and debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural flexibility in exchange for contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: In exchange for the 'unsettling' of decisions (which allows multiple constituencies to 'prevail'), agencies would be permitted to make decisions with far less procedural constraint than they currently can, allowing quick pivots in response to political contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade-offs that reduce formal procedural burdens (e.g., streamlined rulemaking) while increasing opportunities for adversarial challenge and public contestation; balance speed/adaptability against accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of marginalized perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative agon would take far more seriously the perspectives of marginalized groups and individuals, giving them a voice in decisionmaking even when they lack practical access to the levers of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt targeted measures to amplify marginalized voices (outreach, lowered participation barriers, voice-enhancing procedures) so contestation genuinely represents diverse views of the demos rather than perpetuating existing power imbalances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattened bureaucratic hierarchy to foster competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than structuring legitimacy around clarified lines of authority tied to electorally accountable officials, the administrative agon would structure democratic legitimacy around a flattened bureaucratic hierarchy that fosters intra- and interagency competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional structures that decentralize authority across agencies and programs to encourage internal competition and contestation rather than rigid top-down control; evaluate changes for effects on responsiveness and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural openness and interest representation (pluralist ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic legitimacy can be imparted by making agencies open to public participation from diffuse regulatory beneficiaries—an 'interest representation' or pluralist model where policy outcomes reflect fair competition among concerned interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and design participation mechanisms (public notice, comment opportunities, information disclosure) intended to allow a marketplace of influence so that affected interests can mobilize and compete; be mindful of empirical limits to fair competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment rulemaking safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and statutes require agencies to describe proposals in detail before seeking public comment, disclose relied-on materials (Portland Cement doctrine), respond to all significant comments, and avoid making significant post-comment changes without restarting notice-and-comment (logical-outgrowth doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rulemakings, check for: adequate description of proposals, disclosure of supporting materials, substantive responses to significant comments, and adherence to doctrines preventing significant unannounced shifts; these procedural steps are meant to enable effective participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial 'hard look' arbitrary-and-capricious review
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 706 review (arbitrary and capricious) evolved into a 'hard look' standard where courts probe agencies' justifications of policy choices, giving agency decisions a searching review to ensure adequate reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess agency decisions for reasoned explanation, consideration of alternatives, and responsiveness to evidence and comments; recognize that rigorous judicial scrutiny is used as a mechanism to incentivize agencies to take participation seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded access to judicial review (standing liberalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts liberalized barriers to litigation by allowing more groups to obtain standing to sue and challenge agency action, increasing opportunities for judicial oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate statutory and doctrinal access to courts as a democratic accountability mechanism; consider who can bring suits and whether standing rules enable disadvantaged constituencies to challenge agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory enforcement mechanisms (citizen suits and deadlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enacted citizen-suit provisions and strict deadlines for rulemaking to empower private actors to enforce laws or compel agencies to act, aiming to check captured agencies and ensure compliance with congressional mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure administrative legitimacy by the availability and effectiveness of statutory tools allowing private enforcement and temporal constraints that reduce agency delay or inaction; consider how these tools interact with incentives and capture risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the 'procedure fetish'—risks of ossification and information capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques warn that more procedure is not always better: extensive process can cause ossification (slowing adaptive policymaking) and informational capture (regulated entities can overload participatory processes with their resources and expertise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending or evaluating procedural expansion, weigh benefits for participation and legitimacy against risks of ossification, delay, and capture; design procedural rules to mitigate resource asymmetries and informational dominance by regulated interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address power imbalances in participatory mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Pluralist and public-choice critiques highlight that participatory processes often reflect skewed distributions of power—e.g., 'the heavenly chorus sings with a strong upper-class accent'—so formal openness does not guarantee fair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether participation mechanisms actually equalize opportunity to influence (by reducing cost barriers, improving outreach, and countering resource asymmetries) rather than merely formalizing access that advantaged interests exploit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican/deliberative legitimacy (common-good assent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Republican theory emphasizes that legitimacy requires assent from self-governing, civically engaged citizens who recognize laws as good for the polity (a deliberative common good), not mere aggregation of preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess administrative processes for their capacity to cultivate civic engagement and deliberation that can produce broad assent to policies seen as furthering the common good; consider institutional designs that promote deliberative quality, not only participation quantity.
